Composite aircraft structures are vulnerable to barely visible impact damage (BVID) caused by low-velocity impacts such as tool drops or hailstorms.
Three composite structures tested were: GFRP laminated composite, Al-GFRP-Al multilayered composite, and CFRP composite from a military aircraft stabilizer.
PZT transducers with 5 mm diameter and 0.4 mm thickness were embedded in the symmetry plane of specimens.
Impact energies applied were 3 J, 6 J, and 9 J to induce damage.
Damage Indices (DI) based on signal correlation and energy distribution were used to detect damage from PZT sensor signals.
Averaged Damage Indices (ADI) combine multiple PZT sensor readings to provide a qualitative damage indication.
Ultrasonic inspection used a 5 MHz single transducer and phased array techniques to create C-scan images showing damage.
Thermographic inspection used a xenon lamp heat source and a FLIR SC 7000 IR camera with 54.71 Hz frame rate and 5 kJ excitation energy.
Thermography detected delaminations by observing elevated temperatures due to heat transfer barriers.
Vibration-based inspection employed laser Doppler vibrometers to measure modal shapes and frequency response functions in the 0–1.6 kHz range.
Damage detection via vibration analysis used wavelet transforms to identify singularities in modal shapes.
Aluminum face sheets in Al-GFRP-Al composites showed plastic deformation visible in ultrasonic C-scans.
PZT-based methods require baseline signals for comparison and are sensitive to transducer coupling and environmental conditions.
The study confirms that combining multiple NDT methods improves detection accuracy and damage characterization.
Embedded PZT networks can potentially enable continuous in-flight structural health monitoring.
Low-velocity impacts cause matrix cracking and delaminations that reduce residual strength and durability.
Thermographic inspection parameters were selected based on aircraft maintenance experience for optimal damage detection.
The CFRP structure tested contained rivet holes and delaminations typical of operational damage.
Ultrasonic guided wave techniques are widely used for BVID detection due to their sensitivity and localization capabilities.
Vibration-based damage detection is effective but requires dense measurement points and advanced signal processing.
